questions.q: Why does this lesson describe a leaked pipeline secret as arguably worse than a leaked human password?
options: A pipeline secret typically has standing permission to modify production infrastructure directly, with no MFA prompt in the way
Pipeline secrets are always encrypted twice, so this is incorrect
Human passwords never need to be rotated, unlike pipeline secrets
Pipelines never have any permissions beyond reading log files
questions.explain: A long-lived pipeline credential often carries broad, standing permissions to deploy or modify production infrastructure, and unlike a human login, there is no MFA challenge in the way if it is stolen.

questions.q: What makes a managed identity different from a stored cloud credential in a secrets store?
options: A managed identity is just a stored credential with a longer expiration date
A managed identity requires the pipeline to manually request and store a new key every day
A managed identity only works for human users, not automated workloads

A managed identity is assigned directly to a cloud resource by the platform, which issues and rotates the underlying token automatically, so there is no credential a human or script ever sees or stores
questions.explain: With a managed identity, code on the resource asks the platform's metadata endpoint for a token when needed; there is nothing in a config file or environment variable for an attacker to find.

questions.q: What problem does OIDC federation solve for a CI/CD pipeline that runs on infrastructure the CI/CD vendor controls, not the cloud platform?
options: It eliminates the need for the cloud platform to verify anything at all
It requires storing a long-lived credential in the CI/CD platform's secrets store instead of using a managed identity
It lets the cloud platform trust a short-lived OIDC token the CI/CD platform already issues, exchanging it for its own access token with no stored secret involved
It only applies to pipelines running inside a virtual machine the organization owns
questions.explain: Since there's no cloud resource to attach a managed identity to, OIDC federation lets the cloud platform trust a token the CI/CD platform already issued, asserting facts like the branch and repository the run came from, and exchange it for a short-lived cloud credential.

questions.q: What is the underlying shift described for both managed identity and OIDC federation?
options: Removing the need for any cloud platform to issue tokens
Replacing a shared secret both sides must keep safe with a federated trust relationship verified cryptographically on every request
Replacing all encryption with plaintext credentials for simplicity
Making pipeline secrets permanent instead of short-lived
questions.explain: Both mechanisms move away from a static shared secret toward trust based on verifying assertions from a known issuer every time, rather than trusting a static value indefinitely.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call CI/CD pipelines and automated scripts 'workload identities' deserving the same zero-trust treatment as people?
options: Because pipelines are legally required to have a human username
Because workload identity only applies to database administrators
Because automation never actually needs to authenticate to anything
Because automated workloads still authenticate to APIs and deploy infrastructure, so the same never-trust-always-verify principle applies, just using credentials not designed for a human to type
questions.explain: A pipeline still needs to prove who it is before it can deploy infrastructure or push a container image — workload identity is that same verification principle, applied to non-human actors.
